import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class WavBuffer(nn.Module):

model = WavBuffer(10)

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Saved tensor hooks are very useful in terms of providing flexibility in terms of controlling what we can do with a tensor when it is saved for backwards. For example, these hooks can be used to implement checkpointing and offload of intermediate tensors to CPU.
It would be useful to be able to nest these hooks, for example to implement both activation offloading to CPU and saved tensor hooks-based checkpointing. For example, we could have a model structure such as
model = nn.Sequential(checkpoint(layer1), ... checkpoint(layer_n))

and want to offload outer activations to CPU, such as
with save_on_cpu():
    outputs = model(inputs)

This would require saved tensor hooks to be nested. A concrete way of implementing something like this would be to stash the outer hooks, override the hooks with the inner ones during the course of their execution, and then pop/unstash when the inner hooks are finished executing.

class ProcessException(Exception):

        self.error_index = error_index

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Maybe this should've been obvious, but based on striding of the input Tensor, nn.Conv2d can run 20x faster/slower on the GPU. This was quite tricky to debug for us, because the actual change looked innocuous (basically just an extra transpose tucked away somewhere) yet had a huge performance penalty.
Would it be possible to for PyTorch to automatically flag such "inefficient convolution" settings (either as a general-purpose warning or using a special "performance mode")? That would make tracking these types of changes down much faster.
Alternatives
Aside from some tool to emit warnings (or emitting them in general), I suppose that we could also make the performance penalty smaller, although I'm not sure how easy/hard that would be.
Additional context
This was the code that we were running, where we basically needed to unflatten some data before feeding them to a 2D convolution. It turns out that how you unflatten this has some huge performance differences though:
import torch
from torch import nn
from tqdm.auto import tqdm

X = torch.rand(32, 800, 192).to("cuda")

class Permute(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, from_dims: str, to_dims: str) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._permute_idx: List[int] = [from_dims.index(d) for d in to_dims]

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return x.permute(self._permute_idx)
        
### FAST ORDER (81 iterations / second)
network = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Unflatten(dim=-1, unflattened_size=(12, 16)),
    Permute("NTCW", "NCTW"),
    nn.Conv2d(12, 12, kernel_size=(51, 1)),
).to("cuda")

torch.cuda.empty_cache()
for __ in tqdm(range(100)):
    out = network.forward(X)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

### Slow Order (3.79 iterations / second)
network = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Unflatten(dim=-1, unflattened_size=(16, 12)),
    Permute("NTWC", "NCTW"),
    nn.Conv2d(12, 12, kernel_size=(51, 1)),
).to("cuda")
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
for __ in tqdm(range(100)):
    out = network.forward(X)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

Activation checkpointing is an important technique to trade off compute for more GPU memory, thereby enabling larger batch sizes or the training of larger models.
It is especially relevant in the case of large model training with FullyShardedDataParallel, where the goal is to train models that are much bigger than what can fit in a single GPU by using a variety of techniques: sharding, activation offloading, parameter and gradient offloading.
As a result, we would like to add the following APIs to torch.utils.checkpoint:


A checkpoint_wrapper function that wraps an nn.Module instance so that it is always run with checkpointing. This is helpful so that the user will not have to call checkpoint everytime the model's forward pass is run in code. It also allows for better composition with FSDP and DDP, i.e. the user can choose whether to do FSDP(checkpoint_wrapper(model)) or checkpoint_wrapper(FSDP(model)), which, depending on model and other training conditions can have different performance implications. A prototype of checkpoint_wrapper has been added with this PR: #69955, and we would like to upstream this to torch.utils.checkpoint. The implementation is derived from fairscale's checkpoint_wrapper.


Support for activation offloading. To understand this, assume that we have the following model structure: nn.Sequential(checkpoint_wrapper(l1), checkpoint_wrapper(l2), ..., checkpoint_wrapper(ln)). In this case, inner activations are within each checkpointed layer and memory is saved by discarding and recomputing them. Although there are still so-called outer activations between the layers that need to be saved on GPU for recomputation. activation offloading refers to the idea of offloading these activations to CPU to additionally save on GPU memory. It is especially helpful when outer activations are very large. A prototype for activation offloading is here: #70024. The implementation is derived from fairscale's checkpoint_wrapper


In addition, there are 2 checkpoint-based implementations, the traditional reentrant-backwards passed one and the recently added (#69508) checkpoint based on saved tensor hooks. We would like to support both APIs for the time being, because reentrant-based checkpoint is still the default offering and used by FSDP, DDP as well, although we will migrate to saved tensor hooks based checkpointing in the future.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I'm building and distributing a PyTorch extension that requires the nightly version of PyTorch (because it needs fixes that are only in master). Since PyTorch doesn't guarantee ABI compatibility I need to rebuild the extension for each new nightly release, so I did set up a cron job that does that and publishes the package on conda. Each of these packages has a "pinned" dependency on the exact PyTorch version it was built against.
The fact that PyTorch deletes all old nightly binaries whenever it uploads a new one is creating issues to me, because it means users won't be able to install my extension until the time when I build a new version. (Because they can either find the old version of my extension but not of PyTorch, or the new version of PyTorch but not of my extension). I can increase the frequency of my cron job to mitigate this, but there will always inevitably be a gap.
It would be much easier if PyTorch kept the last two versions of the package around, so that until I rebuild my extension for the new nightly my users can still obtain the old nightly of PyTorch.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
It would be great if some of linear algebra operations can be done in parallel using the distributed module.
I am in particular interested in least squares lstsq, but I suppose the argument applies to many linalg ops as well.
torch.linalg.lstsq -> torch.distributed.linalg.lstsq
torch.linalg.* -> torch.distributed.linalg.*

In many large scale applications pieces of a matrix are built on different processes in a distributed environment.
Currently, if I am not wrong, these pieces should be gathered in a single process and solved (with 1 process).
But, first, all of the processes can contribute on solving the problem.
And second, although some communication is still needed, it may eliminate the need to send pieces of matrix between processes.
I suppose there are two ways to approach this:

use SCALAPACK which implements more or less the same existing algorithms in parallel
algorithms which are specifically designed for the distributed setup: e.g. arXiv:1709.10157

This is in particular highly desired in HPC setup with massive parallelism in the field of computational physics and chemistry.
Alternatives
SCALAPCK

🐛 Describe the bug
I'm trying to train https://github.com/JingyunLiang/SwinIR - it's a Swin Transformer used for Image Reconstruction. As such it has one transformer token per pixel, which leads to very large input tensors like [1, 1024*1024, 128]. Running these through LayerNorm(128) is extremely non-performant, to the point of being unusable.
Running the example code below, I get the following pie-chart in tensorboard - LayerNorm takes >90% of the time:

The poor SM efficiency can be seen for the main culprit GammaBetaBackwardCUDAKernel, called as part of aten::native_layer_norm_backward:

Code to reproduce:
import time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.profiler import tensorboard_trace_handler


class TestNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc_in = nn.Linear(3, 128)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList()
        for i in range(0, 10):
            self.layers.append(nn.Linear(128, 128))
            self.layers.append(nn.LayerNorm(128))
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(128, 3)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.fc_in(x)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        x = self.fc_out(x)
        return x


device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
net = TestNet().to(device).train()
in_data = torch.zeros([1, 1024 * 1024, 3]).to(device)
criterion = nn.MSELoss().to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), 0.01)

with torch.profiler.profile(
        schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=2, active=6, repeat=1, skip_first=2),
        on_trace_ready=tensorboard_trace_handler("tmp/profile"),
        with_stack=True, with_flops=True, with_modules=True) as profiler:
    t0 = time.time()
    for i in range(0, 20):
        print(f"step: {i:,d} {time.time() - t0:.3f}")
        out_data = net(in_data)
        loss = criterion(out_data, in_data)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        profiler.step()
print("Done! ")
Please make LayerNorm performant on this type of input, thanks!

🐛 Describe the bug
In python 3.10, subclasses of torch.utils.data.IterableDataset cannot be checked in isinstance versus IterableDataset:
>>> from torch.utils.data import IterableDataset

>>> class SubIterableDataset(IterableDataset):
...    pass

True
